I'm going to give a contrarian take on Neoclouds like $NBIS and say the theme looks compelling after the valuation crash. 

Since there's a reason why Elon's $SPCX is heavily focused on this market full of "guppies" that would die: 

He sees how attractive the economics are after selling compute to $GOOGL and Anthropic. 

And this is reflected by his actions not words, from SpaceX's recent $40B financing for GPUs procurement. 
$AMZN, $MSFT, and even $META also see how profitable the economics are and are accelerating their AI DC buildouts. 

I'd argue if a Neocloud has: 

- Close relationships with $NVDA + others for allocations
- Existing contracted capacity + permitting
- Well funded counterparties, such as Hyperscalers. 
- Attractive economics, such as financing their procurement correctly (not the way $CRWV has with high debt interest unless they refinance). 

Then I think they'll do just fine... 

However, the bigger worry is more toward newer players starting financing or the permitting process, since barrier to entry has now become extremely high. 

For financing, read through on $IREN earnings has shown public Neoclouds can adapt extremely well to tight markets:

As seen with their 90% prepayments for GPU capex on a 5Y deal. 

Their older H100 GPUs recontracted at double their previous pricing and 12% higher contracted pricing also point against depreciation fears. 

And in the case DC buildouts slow from permitting delays... it heavily favors some over others. 

Rosenblatt's recent note for example stated they see little risk with $NBIS primary buildout that was in Missouri, Pennsylvania, and South Carolina. 

And there's probably less risk with developers in places like Australia. 

Markets have also show this infinite compute arbitrage can't go on forever, hence the reluctance to further finance capex, via things like ATMs. 

But ironically, tighter financing and hypothetical restrictive permitting would increase the competitive advantage of established neoclouds. 

And create a larger moat against newer DC developers.

RE: The claim that TSMC will enter memory and disrupt the big three memory makers

This doesn't make sense. As far as I know, TSMC has been working on this project for more than five years, but it would be a mistake to assume what they're building is commodity DRAM. TSMC has no DRAM IP, no DRAM patents, and none of the relevant technology.

I think the term "3D DRAM" is what's causing the misunderstanding.

After talking with industry experts, I believe this is the correct way to read the reports of TSMC entering DRAM.

TSMC's earlier published research gives a good sense of the direction.

At the 2025 VLSI Symposium, TSMC presented a memory technology based on oxide semiconductors, using a cell made of one transistor and one capacitor (1T1C). The goal was to integrate this memory into advanced logic chips and give processors a cache with low power and low latency.

The key feature of the design is that the memory array is built directly into the back end of line (BEOL) interconnect layers of the logic chip. Conventional DRAM is manufactured as a separate chip.

To build the memory array in the interconnect layers of an advanced logic chip, TSMC used select transistors with an oxide semiconductor channel and capacitors fabricated with a low temperature process.

According to TSMC, the test chip, which integrates memory and logic on a single die, operated at 0.75V. Data retention exceeded 128ms, random read/write cycle time was under 8ns, and endurance was above 10¹⁴ cycles. TSMC positioned the technology as a processor cache that offers higher density than SRAM while keeping power consumption and latency low.

So TSMC would be producing 3D DRAM as a next generation technology to replace SRAM. And not in large volumes, either.

Anyone saying TSMC will make DDR or LPDDR has no idea what they're talking about.

I'd like to believe LTAs are durable too. But take one example.

Analog chipmaker onsemi said this in 2023.
On January 5, 2023, at JPMorgan's CES forum, CEO Hassane El-Khoury was asked how much LTSAs would still hold once the shortage eased. His answer: “They are a legally binding agreement ’cause they’re a liability for the customer because they’re take or pay.” He also said he would not accept a customer reopening price talks just because it could get the same parts 10% cheaper elsewhere.

On October 30, 2023, on the Q3 earnings call, onsemi cut its SiC shipment forecast for the year from $1 billion to more than $800 million after one automotive OEM reduced demand. An analyst asked how this could happen when the company had been saying its LTSAs were legally binding. The same CEO reaffirmed that they were binding, but said he did not want to enforce the contracts just to push inventory onto a customer whose demand had dropped. If it worked for both sides, terms could be adjusted customer by customer, whether by a quarter, a year, or longer.

In its 10-K filings, onsemi also states that it amended LTSAs with some strategic customers by mutual agreement in 2024, and changed delivery schedules and committed volumes on some LTSAs in 2025 as demand shifted.

Microchip is another case. Customers in its Preferred Supply Program (PSP) originally had to place 12 months of orders and could not cancel or reschedule them unless Microchip raised prices. On its November 2025 earnings call, however, the CEO said the company had accepted some cancellations and pushouts so customers could adjust their backlog. On the same call, the CFO separately addressed the multiyear LTSAs the company had signed. Some of those contracts were still in effect, he said, but customers had been allowed to defer taking delivery of committed volumes by one to two years if they needed to.

Every time I see cases like these, I doubt how much memory makers' LTAs will protect earnings in a downcycle. Right now the most reliable thing is the prepayments and deposits themselves. That cash can go into capacity expansion today.

I can picture hyperscalers with no DRAM inventory continuing to buy at current prices. But once inventory has piled up, will they keep taking every committed unit at the same price? I have a hard time picturing memory makers holding customers to the high contract price all the way through.

The LTA itself may never be broken and may stay in place. But if both sides agree to push this year's volumes into next year or two years out, this year's earnings estimates come down. If price gets renegotiated too, margin estimates have to come down as well.

Again, I agree LTAs are sturdier than they used to be. What I question is whether, after demand turns, memory makers can still earn 80% margins on contracts signed during the upturn and keep collecting hundreds of billions of dollars in profit because of those LTAs.

【美股复盘 · 11月5日】

**大市**

美股四大指数全线大跌。纳指(QQQ)收于647.05，跌6.49%，为跌幅最深的一个。标普(SPY)收于733.00，跌4.41%。罗素小型股(IWM)收于271.00，跌4.58%。道指(DIA)收于514.32，跌3.52%，相对抗跌。市宽极度一边倒，107只观察股中仅7只上涨、100只下跌。这7只里还包含SOXS、SQQQ、SPXU三只做空型ETF，个股真正上涨的只有 $APP 、BABA、COST，外加黄金ETF GLD涨0.81%。

**板块**

抛压集中在半导体与AI算力投入这一层。跌幅前十全部来自该链条：SNDK跌22.26%领跌，AAOI跌20.89%，AEHR跌19.20%，LITE跌18.68%，CRDO跌17.71%，SMTC跌17.50%，MU跌17.46%，WDC跌17.35%，AMD跌17.26%，算力租赁的IREN跌16.95%。存储、光模块、设备、自建算力这几类单日跌幅均超过16%，呈现整层被统一定价的特征。与之对应，三倍做空半导体的SOXS涨38.98%，是全场涨幅最大的品种;SQQQ涨19.23%,SPXU涨13.23%。杠杆ETF的收盘再平衡机制在这种单边日会放大尾盘波动——三倍基金须在收盘前把敞口调回目标倍数，指数单日大跌时多头杠杆产品被迫减仓,方向与当日跌势一致。防御端COST涨1.83%，MCD跌0.78%、LOW跌0.93%、ADBE跌0.82%，跌幅均不足1%,明显跑赢大市。

**焦点**

APP收涨31.04%，是全市场唯一大幅逆势的个股，主因是前一交易日盘后发布的财报。广告技术这条线与硬件资本开支的定价逻辑不同,在整层算力股被抛售时获得独立的业绩驱动。同一时段公布财报的还有ARM、COHR、QCOM，均已反映在今日盘中。BABA涨2.64%，是上涨名单中表现最稳的非ETF品种之一。盘后AAOI、IONQ、IREN、NET将发布财报，相关影响要到下一个交易日才体现。

**小结**

这是一次结构清晰的单层出清：承担资本开支的硬件与算力环节被集体重定价,跌幅普遍在17%以上;现金流确定的消费与软件名字只是小幅走弱;黄金小幅上涨。市宽100比7，说明卖压并非个股事件,而是对整个AI投入周期的久期重估。业绩成为唯一能对冲这轮抛压的变量——APP证明了这一点。盘后财报密集，半导体与算力链能否企稳,要看下一个交易日。
